tool.name: Ruby on Rails
tool.tagline: Convention-over-configuration Ruby framework for full-stack web apps
tool.description: Ruby on Rails is a full-stack web framework built on the MVC pattern: Active Record for data, Action Controller and Action View for requests and HTML, Hotwire for interactive front ends, plus built-in jobs, mail, caching and WebSockets. Its conventions let small teams ship complete products quickly, and it runs companies like Shopify, GitHub and Basecamp. Rails 8 adds a built-in authentication generator, database-backed queues and caches, and Kamal deployments.

glossary.def: Model-view-controller: splitting an app into models (the data and its rules), views (what the user sees) and controllers (code that takes a request, uses models and picks a view).
Rails' rule that if you name things the standard way, such as an Article model for an articles table, everything connects by itself with no settings to write.
A bin/rails generate command that creates files following Rails' conventions, such as a model with its migration, or a scaffold with everything for one resource.
An interactive Ruby prompt with your whole app loaded, so you can try models and queries by typing them.
Rails 8's built-in tools for background jobs (Solid Queue), caching (Solid Cache) and live updates (Solid Cable), all storing their data in your ordinary database.
Rails' tool for putting an app live on your own servers: it packs the app into a container, copies it to the servers and switches traffic to the new version.
In Rails, a line in config/routes.rb that connects an HTTP method and a URL path, such as GET /articles, to a controller action.
In Rails routing, one kind of thing the app manages, such as articles. resources :articles creates the seven standard routes for listing, showing, creating, editing and deleting them.
A method Rails creates for each named route, like article_path(@article), that returns the right URL so you never type paths by hand.
In Rails, a class whose public methods (actions) answer requests for one kind of thing, such as ArticlesController for articles.
One public method of a Rails controller, such as show or create, that handles one kind of request.
The hash-like object in a Rails controller holding everything the request sent: parts of the URL, query-string values and form fields.
A one-off message such as 'Article saved' that Rails keeps for exactly the next request, usually shown after a redirect.
A Rails controller setting that runs a method before chosen actions, such as loading the record they all need.
Embedded Ruby: HTML files with <%= %> and <% %> tags that run Ruby to fill in the page. Rails views are ERB files ending in .html.erb.
In Rails, the template file that produces the HTML (or JSON) sent back for an action, kept under app/views.
The ERB file that wraps every page of a Rails app with the shared parts, such as the <html> skeleton, header and footer.
A reusable piece of a Rails view kept in its own file whose name starts with an underscore, such as _article.html.erb.
A Ruby method available inside Rails views, such as link_to or pluralize, that produces a bit of HTML or formatted text.
In Rails, a Ruby class, such as Article, that stands for one database table and holds the rules for that data. Each object of it is one row.
The part of Rails that connects models to database tables, so you create, read, update and delete rows with Ruby methods instead of SQL.
A Rails query under construction, returned by where, order and similar. It runs no SQL until you ask for results, so you can keep adding to it.
A Ruby method whose name ends in !, which in Rails means it raises an error on failure instead of quietly returning false: save!, create!, update!.
The Rails helper that builds an HTML form, picking the right URL and method from the model you give it.
Rails' rule that a controller must list which form fields may be saved into a model, so a visitor can't sneak in extra ones like admin=true.
Setting many model attributes at once from a hash, as Article.new(params) does. Rails only allows it for permitted parameters.
A rule declared on a Rails model, such as validates :title, presence: true, that is checked before saving. If it fails, nothing is written.
A method Rails runs at a set moment in a record's life, such as before validation, after saving or after the transaction commits.
A declared link between two Rails models, such as an article having many comments, which adds methods like article.comments.
A model, such as Tagging, that stands for the table linking two others in a many-to-many relationship.
Telling Active Record up front which associated records you'll need, so it loads them in one or two extra queries instead of one query per record.
The slow pattern of one query for a list plus one more query per item, as when printing each article's author without eager loading.
In Rails, a named, reusable piece of a query declared on a model, such as scope :published, that chains with other query methods.
Rails' default approach to interactive pages: the server keeps sending HTML, and Turbo and Stimulus update parts of the page without a full reload.
The Hotwire library that speeds up page changes: Drive swaps whole pages, Frames update one region, and Streams add, replace or remove elements.
A small JavaScript library in Hotwire that attaches behaviour to HTML elements through data- attributes, for the bits HTML can't do alone.
Rails' built-in way to push live updates from the server to open browser pages over a connection that stays open.
The Rails 8 command bin/rails generate authentication, which writes a complete sign-in system (User, Session, controllers) into your app.
A one-line Rails model setting that stores passwords safely as bcrypt digests and adds an authenticate method.
A Rails class that holds values for the request being handled right now, such as the signed-in user, reachable from anywhere in the app.
In Rails tests, a named sample record defined in a YAML file under test/fixtures and loaded into the test database, such as articles(:published).
A Rails test that drives a real browser through the app, clicking and typing like a user. Slow but checks everything including JavaScript.
Rails' standard way to write background jobs: a class with a perform method, queued with perform_later and run later by a worker.
A short reference like gid://app/Invoice/42 that Active Job stores instead of a whole record, loading the record fresh when the job runs.
Saving the rendered HTML of part of a page under a key, so the next request reuses it instead of rendering it again.
Rails' caching approach: the cache key includes the record's last-updated time, so when the record changes a new key is used and the old entry is simply ignored.
A Rails template format (.json.jbuilder) for describing the JSON a view should return, line by line in Ruby.
A Ruby module written with ActiveSupport::Concern that packages shared behaviour, such as being archivable, for several Rails models or controllers to include.
A plain old Ruby object: a class with no Rails parent, used for logic that doesn't belong to a database table.
A plain Ruby class that includes ActiveModel::Model to get validations and form support, for forms that don't match one table.
A plain Ruby class that performs one multi-step task, such as Checkout.new(cart, user).call, when the work doesn't belong to a single model.
The loader Rails uses to find classes: it works out from a file's path which constant it must define, so you never write require for your own files.
Loading a Ruby file automatically the first time its class or module is used, based on the file's name and folder.
In development, Rails forgetting your app's classes when a file changes and loading them again on the next request, so edits show without a restart.
A Ruby file in config/initializers that runs once while the app starts, for settings and setup.
The hook a gem uses to plug into Rails' start-up, adding its own settings, initializers or routes.
The small standard that connects Ruby web servers and frameworks: an app is any object with a call(env) method returning status, headers and body.
The chain of small Rack layers a request passes through before reaching the Rails router, each handling one shared job such as cookies, sessions or logging.
The web server Rails uses by default: it accepts connections and runs your app in several processes and threads at once.
A small proxy Rails 8 puts in front of Puma in production, adding HTTP/2, compression and fast serving of static files.
One of the separate processes Puma starts, each running a copy of the app; roughly one per CPU core.
A Puma setting that loads the app once before splitting into workers, so the workers share that memory.
Ruby's built-in just-in-time compiler, which speeds up Ruby code while it runs; Rails turns it on when available.
Application performance monitoring: a service that records how long each request, query and job takes in production, so you can find the slow parts.

concepts.name: Creating an app and its conventions
concepts.summary: Create a Rails 8 app, run it in your browser, and learn the folder structure and the naming conventions that make Rails work.
concepts.why: Rails' conventions are the framework: knowing them tells you where everything is and what you get for free.
concepts.body:
A website works like this: your **browser** sends a **request** ("give me the page at /articles") to a program on another computer, the **web server**, which sends back a **response**: usually a page written in **HTML**, the text format browsers turn into what you see. Rails is a **framework** for writing that server-side program in Ruby: a large ready-made structure where you fill in your own parts and Rails decides when to call them.

Install Rails with `gem install rails` and create an app with `rails new blog`. The defaults are deliberately simple: the database is SQLite, a database kept in a single file, so there's nothing to install. The page code that runs in the browser works without any extra build step. Work that runs later in the background, saved copies of pages for speed, and live updates (the **Solid** tools) keep their data in that same database too. Rails also writes the files needed to put the app on a real server later (a Dockerfile and **Kamal** settings) and a basic set of code checks.

Run `bin/dev` (or `bin/rails server`) and open `http://localhost:3000` in your browser: `localhost` means your own computer.

The folders follow **MVC**, model-view-controller, a way of splitting an app into three kinds of parts:
- `app/models`: the data and its rules. `app/views`: the pages the user sees. `app/controllers`: the code that takes a request, uses the models and picks a view. Also `app/jobs`, `app/mailers`, `app/helpers` and `app/javascript`.
- `config/routes.rb` says which **URL** (web address, such as `/articles/5`) runs which code; `config/database.yml` says how to reach the database; `config/credentials.yml.enc` keeps passwords and keys in encrypted (scrambled) form.
- `db/migrate` and `db/schema.rb` describe the database tables; `test/` holds tests; `bin/` holds the commands you run, like `bin/rails`.

**Convention over configuration** means that if you name things the standard way, they connect by themselves: the `Article` model uses the `articles` table, `ArticlesController` shows pages from `app/views/articles/`, and `app/models/line_item.rb` defines `LineItem`. Follow the conventions and you write almost no glue code.

**Generators** create files that follow them: `bin/rails generate scaffold Article title:string body:text` produces a migration, a model, a controller, views, URL rules and tests for articles in one go. The **Rails console**, `bin/rails console`, opens IRB with your app loaded, so you can try models and queries directly.
concepts.code:
gem install rails
rails new blog            # SQLite database, Hotwire, Solid Queue/Cache/Cable, Kamal
cd blog
bin/rails --version       # Rails 8.0.x

bin/rails generate scaffold Article title:string body:text published:boolean
bin/rails db:migrate      # create the articles table
bin/dev                   # open http://localhost:3000/articles in your browser

bin/rails console         # IRB with the app loaded
# >> Article.create!(title: "Hello", body: "First post")
# >> Article.count  # => 1

bin/rails routes -g article   # routes matching "article"
bin/rails test                # run the tests
takeaways: rails new gives a complete app that stores everything in one database
Names connect the layers: Article -> articles table -> ArticlesController -> views/articles
Generators and bin/rails console speed up everyday work
pitfalls: Fighting conventions (custom table names, odd file names) and then writing glue code Rails would have made unnecessary.

quiz.q: Following Rails conventions, which table does the model LineItem use?
quiz.explain: Model names are singular CamelCase; tables are plural snake_case.

concepts.name: Routing
concepts.summary: Connect URLs to controller actions in config/routes.rb with resources, nested routes, root and path helpers.
concepts.why: Routes define your app's URL design and create the path helpers used throughout views and controllers.
concepts.body:
Every request names an **HTTP method** — what the browser wants to do, such as **GET** to read a page or **POST** to send in a form — and a path, the part of the URL after the site name. A **route** connects one such pair to a **controller action**: a method in one of your controller classes, written `controller#action`. `config/routes.rb` lists them:

```ruby
Rails.application.routes.draw do
  root "articles#index"
  get "/about", to: "pages#about", as: :about
  resources :articles
end
```

`resources :articles` treats articles as a **resource**, a kind of thing the app manages, and creates the seven standard routes for it: `index` (GET /articles, the list), `new` (the empty form), `create` (POST /articles), `show` (GET /articles/:id, one article), `edit`, `update` (PATCH/PUT /articles/:id) and `destroy` (DELETE). Limit them with `only: [:index, :show]` or `except:`. Use `resource :profile` (singular) for things a user has only one of.

Every named route gets **path helpers**: methods that return the right URL. `articles_path` gives `/articles`, `article_path(@article)` gives `/articles/42`, and there are `edit_article_path(@article)` and `new_article_path`; the `_url` versions include the site's address as well. Use them everywhere instead of typing paths.

Organising routes:
- **Nested** resources express ownership: `resources :articles do resources :comments, only: [:create, :destroy] end` gives `/articles/:article_id/comments`. Keep nesting one level deep (use `shallow: true` for deeper hierarchies).
- `member { post :publish }` adds `/articles/:id/publish` for one article; `collection { get :search }` adds `/articles/search` for all of them.
- `namespace :admin do ... end` puts `/admin` in front of paths, helpers and controller names (`Admin::UsersController`).
- Dynamic segments and constraints: `get "/u/:username", to: "users#show", constraints: { username: /[a-z0-9_]+/ }`.

`bin/rails routes` lists everything, with `-g` to filter. Routes are tried top to bottom; the first match wins.
concepts.code:
# config/routes.rb
Rails.application.routes.draw do
  root "articles#index"

  resources :articles do
    member { post :publish }               # POST /articles/:id/publish
    collection { get :search }             # GET  /articles/search
    resources :comments, only: %i[create destroy]
  end

  resource :session                        # singular: /session
  get "/@:username", to: "profiles#show", as: :profile,
      constraints: { username: /[a-z0-9_]+/ }

  namespace :admin do
    resources :users, only: %i[index update]   # Admin::UsersController
  end

  get "up" => "rails/health#show", as: :rails_health_check
end

# Helpers: article_path(@article)              => "/articles/42"
#          article_comments_path(@article)      => "/articles/42/comments"
#          publish_article_path(@article)       => "/articles/42/publish"
#          profile_path(username: "ada")        => "/@ada"
takeaways: resources :things creates the seven standard routes and their helpers
Use path helpers like article_path(@article) instead of typing URLs
Nest one level for ownership; use member, collection and namespace to organise
pitfalls: Nesting resources several levels deep, producing long URLs and helper names; prefer shallow nesting.

quiz.q: Which request does resources :articles map to ArticlesController#update?
quiz.explain: update is reached with PATCH (or PUT) on the member URL /articles/:id.

concepts.name: Controllers and actions
concepts.summary: Write controller actions that read params, load records, and send back a page, a redirect or JSON with the right status.
concepts.why: Controllers handle every request, and knowing render versus redirect and callbacks avoids many beginner bugs.
concepts.body:
A **controller** is a class inheriting from `ApplicationController`; each public method is an **action**. After an action runs, Rails **renders** (builds the HTML of) the **template** with the same name — the page file `articles/show.html.erb` for `show` — unless you call `render` or `redirect_to` yourself. Instance variables set in the action (`@article`) are visible in the template.

**`params`** holds everything the request sent, in one hash-like object: parts of the URL such as `:id`, values from the **query string** (the `?page=2` part of a URL), and form fields. `params[:id]` and `params["id"]` both work. Values are strings.

Responding:
- `render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity` shows a different template in the same request, used to show a form again with its errors. The status is a number sent with every response saying how it went; 422 (unprocessable) tells the browser-side code that the form failed.
- `redirect_to @article, notice: "Saved"` sends a **redirect**: a response telling the browser to request a different URL. The notice is kept in the **flash**, a message store that lasts for exactly the next request. Use `status: :see_other` (303) after a DELETE.
- `render json: @article` sends JSON (a text format for data that programs read); `head :no_content` sends an empty response; `render plain: "ok"` plain text.

A common bug is calling `render` or `redirect_to` twice in one action, which raises `DoubleRenderError`; add `return` after an early redirect.

**`before_action`** runs a method before chosen actions: `before_action :set_article, only: %i[show edit update destroy]` loads the record once for all of them. `rescue_from` handles exceptions per controller.

`Model.find(params[:id])` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` when the record is missing; on the live site Rails turns that into a 404 Not Found page. The browser forgets everything between requests, so to remember things across them use the **session** (`session[:key]`, the server's memory of one visitor) or **cookies** (small values the browser stores and sends back each time).
concepts.code:
class ArticlesController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_article, only: %i[show edit update destroy]

  def index
    @articles = Article.order(created_at: :desc).limit(20)
  end

  def show; end   # renders app/views/articles/show.html.erb

  def update
    if @article.update(article_params)
      redirect_to @article, notice: "Article updated"
    else
      render :edit, status: :unprocessable_entity
    end
  end

  def destroy
    @article.destroy!
    redirect_to articles_path, notice: "Deleted", status: :see_other
  end
  private
  def set_article = @article = Article.find(params[:id])   # 404 if missing
  def article_params = params.expect(article: %i[title body])
end
takeaways: Actions render the template of the same name unless you render or redirect
render shows a page in the same request; redirect_to makes the browser start a new one
before_action shares setup such as loading the record
pitfalls: Calling redirect_to and then continuing to code that renders, causing DoubleRenderError; return after redirecting.

quiz.q: A form submission fails validation. What is the conventional response?
quiz.explain: Rendering keeps the invalid object and its errors; the 422 status tells Turbo to show the response.

concepts.name: Views, layouts and partials
concepts.summary: Build pages with ERB templates, layouts and partials, and use helpers like link_to and the flash.
concepts.why: Views are what users see, and partials and helpers keep pages consistent without repeating yourself.
concepts.body:
A **view** is the file that produces a page. Rails views are **ERB** templates, HTML with Ruby mixed in, kept at `app/views/<controller>/<action>.html.erb`. `<%= expr %>` prints a value into the page; `<% code %>` runs Ruby without printing, for loops and conditionals.

What `<%= %>` prints is **HTML-escaped**: characters such as `<` are converted so the browser shows them as text instead of treating them as HTML. That protects against **XSS**, where an attacker types a script into a comment and it runs in other visitors' browsers. Avoid `raw` and `html_safe` on anything a user typed.

The **layout**, `app/views/layouts/application.html.erb`, wraps every page with the shared skeleton; `<%= yield %>` marks where the action's template goes. Templates can fill named regions with `content_for :title` and the layout reads them with `yield :title`.

**Partials** are reusable fragments whose file names start with an underscore: `_article.html.erb`. Show one with `<%= render "form", article: @article %>` or, for a list of records, `<%= render @articles %>`, which renders `articles/_article` once per record with a local variable `article`. That is faster than looping and calling `render` yourself.

**Helpers** are Ruby methods you can call in views:
- `link_to "Edit", edit_article_path(@article)` makes a link, and `button_to "Delete", @article, method: :delete` a button that sends a DELETE request.
- `image_tag`, `time_ago_in_words`, `pluralize(3, "comment")`, `number_to_currency`, `truncate`, `simple_format`.
- Your own, in `app/helpers`.

Show flash messages in the layout with `notice` and `alert`. Use `dom_id(@article)` for consistent element ids (`article_42`), which Turbo uses as well. Keep logic out of views: compute data in the controller or a model method and give the view simple values.
concepts.code:
<%# app/views/layouts/application.html.erb %> <%= content_for(:title) || "Blog" %> <% if notice %>

<%= notice %>

<% end %> <%= yield %> <%# app/views/articles/index.html.erb %> <% content_for :title, "All articles" %>

Articles (<%= pluralize(@articles.size, "article") %>)

<%= render @articles %> <%# renders _article.html.erb for each %> <%= link_to "New article", new_article_path %> <%# app/views/articles/_article.html.erb %>

<%= link_to article.title, article %>

<%= truncate(article.body, length: 120) %>

<%= time_ago_in_words(article.created_at) %> ago
takeaways: <%= %> prints escaped output; <% %> runs code
Layouts wrap pages via yield; partials (_name) are reusable fragments
render @collection renders a partial per record efficiently
pitfalls: Calling html_safe or raw on something a user typed, which switches off this protection and allows XSS.

quiz.q: What does <%= render @articles %> do?
quiz.explain: Rendering a collection uses the model's partial path, articles/_article, for each element.

concepts.name: Migrations and the schema
concepts.summary: Change the database with migrations, links between tables and indexes, and understand schema.rb.
concepts.why: Migrations keep every environment's database in sync and are part of every Rails feature you build.
concepts.body:
A **migration** is a Ruby class in `db/migrate` that changes the schema. Generate one with a descriptive name and Rails pre-fills it:

```bash
bin/rails generate migration AddPublishedAtToArticles published_at:datetime:index
bin/rails generate model Comment article:references body:text
```

The `change` method describes the change, and Rails knows how to reverse most operations automatically:

- `create_table :comments do |t| ... t.timestamps end`. Tables get an `id` primary key by default.
- `t.references :article, null: false, foreign_key: true` adds an `article_id` column, an index on it, and a **foreign key**: a database rule that every `article_id` must match an existing article.
- `add_column`, `remove_column` (give the type so it stays reversible), `rename_column`, `add_index :users, :email, unique: true`, `change_column_null`, `change_column_default`.
- For irreversible changes, write `up` and `down`, or use `reversible do |dir| ... end`.

Run `bin/rails db:migrate`; `db:rollback` undoes the last one; `db:migrate:status` shows state. `db:prepare` creates the database if needed and migrates it, handy when putting a new version live.

After migrating, Rails dumps the full current schema to `db/schema.rb`. Commit it: it is the authoritative description of the database, and `db:schema:load` builds a fresh database from it far faster than replaying every migration.

Enforce rules in the database too: `null: false`, unique indexes and foreign keys catch problems that checks in Ruby miss, such as two requests inserting the same email at the same moment.
concepts.code:
# db/migrate/20250601120000_create_comments.rb
class CreateComments < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.0]
  def change
    create_table :comments do |t|
      t.references :article, null: false, foreign_key: true
      t.references :user, null: false, foreign_key: true
      t.text :body, null: false
      t.timestamps
    end
    add_index :comments, [:article_id, :created_at]
  end
end

# db/migrate/20250602090000_add_slug_to_articles.rb
class AddSlugToArticles < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.0]
  def change
    add_column :articles, :slug, :string
    add_index :articles, :slug, unique: true
  end
end

# $ bin/rails db:migrate      -> updates db/schema.rb
# $ bin/rails db:rollback     -> reverses AddSlugToArticles automatically
takeaways: Write changes in change; Rails reverses most of them automatically
t.references with foreign_key: true adds the column, index and constraint
Commit db/schema.rb; it is the authoritative schema
pitfalls: Editing a migration that already ran on other machines instead of adding a new one.

quiz.q: What does t.references :article, foreign_key: true create?
options: An article_id column, an index on it and a foreign key to articles
quiz.explain: references adds article_id with an index by default, and foreign_key: true adds the constraint.

concepts.name: Active Record basics
concepts.summary: Create, read, update and delete records with Active Record, and build queries that run only when you need the results.
concepts.why: Active Record is how Rails apps talk to the database, and its query methods are used in nearly every file.
concepts.body:
**Active Record** is the part of Rails that connects models to tables. A **model** is a class inheriting from `ApplicationRecord`. Active Record reads the table's columns and creates a getter and setter for each (an **attribute**), so `class Article < ApplicationRecord; end` is a complete model.

**Create**: `Article.new(title: "Hi")` then `save`, or `Article.create(...)`. **Read**: `find(id)` (raises `RecordNotFound`), `find_by(slug: "hi")` (returns nil), `first`, `last`, `all`. **Update**: `article.update(title: "New")`. **Delete**: `article.destroy` (runs the model's callbacks, covered later) or `delete_all`/`destroy_all` on a set of records.

A model can declare **validations**, rules such as "title must be present", checked before anything is saved (next level). **Bang methods** (`save!`, `create!`, `update!`) raise an error when a validation fails; the plain versions just return false. Use the bang versions where failure would be a bug, such as in scripts.

Query methods chain into a **relation**, which is lazy: no SQL runs until you ask for results with `each`, `to_a`, `first`, `count` or similar.

```ruby
Article.where(published: true).where("created_at > ?", 1.week.ago).order(created_at: :desc).limit(10)
```

- Hash conditions (`where(status: "draft")`, `where(id: [1, 2])`, `where(created_at: 1.day.ago..)`) and `?` placeholders are safe. Never build SQL strings with user input inside them: that is **SQL injection**, where a visitor types SQL into a search box and the database runs it.
- `where.not(...)`, `or(...)`, `select`, `distinct`, `group`, `having`.
- `pluck(:title)` returns plain values without building model objects; `exists?` and `count` run cheap queries.
- `find_each` goes through a big table 1000 rows at a time instead of loading it all.

`.to_sql` shows the SQL a relation will run, and the console and the server's log print every query.
concepts.code:
article = Article.create!(title: "Hello Rails", body: "First", published: true)
article.update!(title: "Hello again")
p article.persisted?                     # true

recent = Article.where(published: true)
                .where(created_at: 1.week.ago..)
                .order(created_at: :desc)
                .limit(5)                # nothing queried yet
puts recent.to_sql
# SELECT "articles".* FROM "articles" WHERE "articles"."published" = 1
#   AND "articles"."created_at" >= '...' ORDER BY ... LIMIT 5
p recent.map(&:title)                    # query runs here

p Article.find_by(title: "nope")         # nil
p Article.where(published: false).count  # SELECT COUNT(*) ...
p Article.pluck(:id, :title).first       # [1, "Hello again"]

term = "Rails"
Article.where("title LIKE ?", "%#{term}%")   # safe: bound parameter
Article.find_each(batch_size: 500) { |a| a.touch }
takeaways: Models map to tables; attributes come from columns automatically
Relations are lazy and chainable; SQL runs when results are needed
Use hash conditions or ? placeholders, never string interpolation
pitfalls: Writing where("title = '#{params[:q]}'"), which lets a visitor inject SQL.

quiz.q: When does Article.where(published: true).order(:title) hit the database?
options: When the results are needed, e.g. each, to_a or first
quiz.explain: Relations are lazy; enumerating or loading them triggers the query.

concepts.name: Forms and strong parameters
concepts.summary: Build forms with form_with, show validation errors, and allow only the expected fields with params.expect.
concepts.why: Forms are how users change data, and strong parameters are Rails' guard against visitors setting fields they shouldn't.
concepts.body:
An HTML form is a set of input boxes with a submit button; pressing it sends the typed values to the server. **`form_with(model: @article)`** builds one for a model. Rails picks the URL and HTTP method by convention: POST to `/articles` for a new record, PATCH to `/articles/:id` for an existing one. Inside the block, **field** helpers make the inputs, named `article[title]` and so on, and fill in current values:

```erb
<%= form_with model: @article do |f| %>
  <%= f.label :title %>
  <%= f.text_field :title %>
  <%= f.text_area :body %>
  <%= f.submit %>
<% end %>
```

Other helpers: `f.select`, `f.check_box`, `f.date_field`, `f.email_field`, `f.file_field`, `f.collection_select`. The form also includes a hidden **CSRF token**, a random code that Rails checks on every non-GET request, so another website can't submit forms in your user's name (**CSRF**, cross-site request forgery).

Show validation errors with `@article.errors.full_messages`, or per field with `@article.errors[:title]`. Inputs that failed are wrapped in a `field_with_errors` element for styling.

The submitted values arrive nested: `params[:article][:title]`. Setting many attributes from a hash at once is **mass assignment**. Passing the raw params to `create` or `update` would let a visitor add a field such as `admin: true` to the form and have it saved, so Rails refuses params that haven't been permitted. **Strong parameters** list what is allowed. Rails 8 adds `params.expect`, which also checks the shape and answers 400 Bad Request for malformed input:

```ruby
params.expect(article: [:title, :body, tag_ids: []])
```

The older equivalent is `params.require(:article).permit(:title, :body, tag_ids: [])`. Arrays and nested hashes must be listed explicitly.
concepts.code:
# app/controllers/articles_controller.rb def new @article = Article.new end def create @article = Current.user.articles.new(article_params) if @article.save redirect_to @article, notice: "Published!" else render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity end end private def article_params # Rails 8: whitelist and check the shape in one call params.expect(article: [:title, :body, :category_id, tag_ids: []]) end # Submitted: { article: { title: "Hi", body: "...", admin: "1" } } # -> admin is filtered out; a non-hash article param -> 400 Bad Request # app/views/articles/_form.html.erb (excerpt) # <% if article.errors.any? %> #
    <% article.errors.full_messages.each do |m| %>
  • <%= m %>
    • <% end %>
# <% end %>
takeaways: form_with(model:) picks the URL, method and field values by convention
Strong parameters list the allowed attributes before mass assignment
params.expect (Rails 8) checks the shape too and returns 400 for bad input
pitfalls: Forgetting to permit array params like tag_ids: [], so they are silently dropped.

quiz.q: Why does Article.create(params[:article]) raise ForbiddenAttributesError?
options: Unfiltered params can't be mass-assigned; you must permit attributes first
quiz.explain: Rails blocks mass assignment of unpermitted parameters so visitors can't set columns of their choosing.

concepts.name: Validations and callbacks
concepts.summary: Validate models before saving, read errors, and use lifecycle callbacks carefully.
concepts.why: Validations keep bad data out, and misused callbacks are one of the most common sources of Rails bugs.
concepts.body:
**Validations** run when you call `save`, `create`, `update` or `valid?`. If any fails, nothing is written and `errors` is populated:

```ruby
validates :title, presence: true, length: { maximum: 120 }
validates :slug, uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false }, format: { with: /\A[a-z0-9-]+\z/ }
validates :price, numericality: { greater_than_or_equal_to: 0 }
```

Other built-ins: `inclusion: { in: %w[draft published] }`, `comparison`, `acceptance`, `confirmation`. Add `allow_nil: true`, `if:`/`unless:` and `on: :create` to limit when they apply. For custom logic, write `validate :method_name` and call `errors.add(:field, "message")`.

`uniqueness` checks with a SELECT before inserting, so two requests arriving at the same moment can both pass. Always back it with a **unique index** in the database.

**Model callbacks** are methods Rails runs at set moments in a record's life: `before_validation`, `before_save`, `after_create`, `before_destroy`, and the transaction-aware `after_commit` (with shortcuts `after_create_commit` and `after_update_commit`). Good uses are small, model-local concerns: normalising data before validation (Rails 7.1+ also has `normalizes :email, with: -> { it.strip.downcase }`) or filling in values computed from others.

Rules for callbacks:

- Use `after_commit` (not `after_save`) for **side effects**, work beyond the save itself such as queuing a job or sending email, so they don't fire for transactions that are later rolled back.
- Don't put cross-model workflows in callbacks; an explicit method or service object is easier to follow and test.
- Methods like `update_column`, `update_all` and `insert_all` skip validations and callbacks.
concepts.code:
class Article < ApplicationRecord
  normalizes :slug, with: -> { it.strip.downcase }

  validates :title, presence: true, length: { maximum: 120 }
  validates :slug, presence: true, uniqueness: true,
                   format: { with: /\A[a-z0-9-]+\z/, message: "only a-z, 0-9 and -" }
  validate :publish_date_not_in_past, if: :published?

  before_validation :generate_slug, on: :create
  after_create_commit -> { NotifyFollowersJob.perform_later(self) }

  private

  def generate_slug = self.slug ||= title.to_s.parameterize
  def publish_date_not_in_past
    errors.add(:published_at, "can't be in the past") if published_at&.past?
  end
end

a = Article.new(title: "", slug: "Bad Slug!")
a.valid?                       # => false
a.errors.full_messages
# => ["Title can't be blank", "Slug only a-z, 0-9 and -"]
Article.create!(title: "Hello World")   # slug "hello-world"; job enqueued after commit
takeaways: save and valid? run validations; errors explains failures
Back uniqueness validations with a unique database index
Use after_commit for side effects; keep callbacks small and local
pitfalls: Sending emails or enqueueing jobs in after_save, which fires even if the transaction later rolls back.

quiz.q: Why can validates :email, uniqueness: true still allow duplicates?
options: Two concurrent requests can both check before either inserts
quiz.explain: The check is a separate SELECT; only a unique index makes the database reject the race.

concepts.name: Associations and eager loading
concepts.summary: Connect models with belongs_to, has_many and has_many :through, and prevent N+1 queries with includes.
concepts.why: Real domains are relational, and N+1 queries are the most common Rails performance problem.
concepts.body:
**Associations** declare how models relate and generate methods for it:

- `belongs_to :author, class_name: "User"` on the model holding the foreign key (`author_id`). Since Rails 5 it is **required** by default; use `optional: true` otherwise.
- `has_many :comments, dependent: :destroy` on the other side. `dependent:` decides what happens to children when the parent is destroyed.
- `has_one :profile`.
- `has_many :tags, through: :taggings` for many-to-many links via a **join model** (`Tagging`, standing for the table of article-tag pairs), which can carry its own columns. `has_and_belongs_to_many` exists but a join model is more flexible.
- Polymorphic: `belongs_to :commentable, polymorphic: true` lets one comments table belong to several kinds of model, such as articles and videos.

Generated methods include `article.comments` (a relation you can chain: `article.comments.where(approved: true)`), `article.comments.create!(...)` (sets the foreign key), `comment.article`, `article.tag_ids = [1, 2]`. `counter_cache: true` on `belongs_to` keeps a `comments_count` column up to date.

The **N+1 problem**: listing 50 articles and calling `article.author.name` in the view runs 51 queries. Fix it with **eager loading**, telling Rails up front which associations you'll need:

- `includes(:author, comments: :user)` lets Rails choose between separate queries and a JOIN.
- `preload` always uses separate queries; `eager_load` always uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN (needed when you filter on the association).
- `joins(:comments)` is for filtering only and doesn't load the association.

Turn on `strict_loading` (per model, per query or app-wide) to raise an error during development whenever an association is loaded on first use rather than eagerly.
concepts.code:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :articles, foreign_key: :author_id, inverse_of: :author
end

class Article < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :author, class_name: "User"
  has_many :comments, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :taggings, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :tags, through: :taggings
end

class Comment < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :article, counter_cache: true   # needs articles.comments_count
  belongs_to :user
end

# N+1: 1 query for articles + 1 per article for its author
Article.limit(50).each { |a| puts a.author.name }

# Eager loaded: 3 queries total
Article.includes(:author, :tags).limit(50).each do |a|
  puts "#{a.title} by #{a.author.name} [#{a.tags.map(&:name).join(', ')}] #{a.comments_count}"
end
Article.joins(:tags).where(tags: { name: "rails" }).distinct   # filter only
Article.strict_loading.first.author   # raises ActiveRecord::StrictLoadingViolationError
takeaways: belongs_to holds the foreign key and is required by default
has_many :through models many-to-many with a real join model
includes/preload/eager_load fix N+1; joins only filters
pitfalls: Calling association methods inside a loop over records loaded without includes.

quiz.q: You need articles WHERE tags.name = 'rails', and you also display each article's tags. Which is right?
quiz.explain: Filtering on the association needs it in the JOIN, and eager_load both joins and loads it.

quiz.q: What does belongs_to :author do if author_id is nil when saving (Rails 5+)?
options: Adds a validation error: Author must exist
quiz.explain: belongs_to is required by default unless you pass optional: true.

concepts.name: Scopes and advanced queries
concepts.summary: Name reusable queries with scopes and class methods, and use joins, grouping, merges and batching.
concepts.why: Named scopes turn scattered query fragments into a readable, composable vocabulary for your domain.
concepts.body:
A **scope** names a query fragment on the model:

```ruby
scope :published, -> { where(published: true) }
scope :recent, ->(days = 7) { where(created_at: days.days.ago..) }
```

Scopes always return a relation, so they chain: `Article.published.recent(30).order(:title)`. They also work through associations: `user.articles.published`. A class method that returns a relation works the same way; scopes are just shorter, and a scope whose body returns nil returns `all` instead, keeping chains safe.

Avoid `default_scope`: it silently applies everywhere, including to associations and new records, and is hard to escape.

More query tools:

- `merge(OtherModel.scope)` reuses another model's scope inside a join: `Article.joins(:author).merge(User.active)`.
- `group(:category_id).count` returns a hash like `{1 => 12, 2 => 5}`; `sum`, `average`, `maximum` work the same way.
- `left_joins(:comments).where(comments: { id: nil })` finds records without children; `where.missing(:comments)` is shorthand.
- `or`, `not`, `rewhere`, `unscope`, `extending`.
- `in_batches(of: 1000).update_all(...)` changes large sets 1000 rows at a time; `insert_all` and `upsert_all` write many rows in one statement (skipping validations and callbacks).
- `Article.where(...).explain` shows the database's **query plan**: how it intends to run the query and which indexes it will use.

For SQL that is easier written raw, `find_by_sql` and `select("...")` remain available, still with bound parameters.
concepts.code:
class Article < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :author, class_name: "User"
  has_many :comments

  scope :published, -> { where(published: true) }
  scope :recent, ->(days = 7) { where(created_at: days.days.ago..) }
  scope :by, ->(user) { where(author: user) if user }   # nil -> all
  scope :popular, -> { joins(:comments).group(:id).having("COUNT(comments.id) >= ?", 10) }
end

class User < ApplicationRecord
  scope :active, -> { where(active: true) }
end

Article.published.recent(30).by(nil).order(:title)   # by(nil) keeps the chain
Article.joins(:author).merge(User.active)             # reuse User's scope
Article.published.group(:category_id).count           # {1 => 12, 2 => 5}
Article.where.missing(:comments)                      # articles with no comments
Article.where(published: false).in_batches(of: 1000)
       .update_all(archived: true)                    # chunked set-based update
Article.upsert_all([{ slug: "a", title: "A" }], unique_by: :slug)
puts Article.published.recent.explain
takeaways: Scopes name reusable query fragments and always return relations
merge reuses another model's scopes across joins
group/count, where.missing, in_batches and upsert_all cover common bulk needs
pitfalls: Using default_scope, which leaks into every query and association.

quiz.q: What does a scope return if its lambda body evaluates to nil?
options: The model's all relation, so chaining still works
quiz.explain: Scopes guarantee a relation; a nil body is replaced with all.

concepts.name: Hotwire: Turbo and Stimulus
concepts.summary: Make server-built pages feel instant with Turbo Drive, Frames and Streams, and add small JavaScript behaviours with Stimulus.
concepts.why: Hotwire is Rails' default front end: interactive pages without writing and maintaining a separate JavaScript app.
concepts.body:
**Hotwire** keeps building pages on the server and sends HTML, not JSON, to the browser. Two libraries come installed by default.

**Turbo** handles navigation and page updates:
- **Turbo Drive** catches link clicks and form submissions, fetches the next page in the background and swaps in its body without a full reload. Failed form submissions must come back with a 4xx status (422) so Turbo shows the response. Turbo 8 can **morph** pages on refresh (`turbo_refreshes_with method: :morph`), changing only what differs and keeping scroll position and focus.
- **Turbo Frames** (`<%= turbo_frame_tag dom_id(article) do %>`) make one region of the page update on its own: links and forms inside a frame replace only that frame with the matching frame from the response. Load a frame only when needed with `src:` and `loading: :lazy`.

- **Turbo Streams** apply targeted changes to the page: `append`, `prepend`, `replace`, `update`, `remove`, `before`, `after`, `refresh`. A controller can respond with them (`format.turbo_stream`), or a model can broadcast them to every open page with `broadcasts_to` or `broadcast_append_to`. Broadcasting uses **Action Cable**, which keeps a connection open from the server to each browser (Solid Cable stores its data in the database).

**Stimulus** adds small bits of JavaScript to server-built HTML. A Stimulus controller is a JavaScript class attached to an element through `data-` attributes: `data-controller="clipboard"`, `data-action="click->clipboard#copy"` and `data-clipboard-target="source"`. Its state lives in the HTML itself, so it keeps working after Turbo replaces content.

The workflow: start with plain server-built pages, add Frames for editing in place, Streams for live updates, and Stimulus only for what HTML can't do.
concepts.code:
<%# app/views/comments/_comment.html.erb %> <%= turbo_frame_tag dom_id(comment) do %>

<%= comment.body %> <%= link_to "Edit", edit_comment_path(comment) %>

<% end %> <%# Edit renders a form inside the same frame id: only this comment is replaced %> <%# app/views/articles/show.html.erb %> <%= turbo_stream_from @article %> <%# subscribe to live updates %>
<%= render @article.comments %>
<%# app/models/comment.rb: after_create_commit -> { broadcast_append_to article, target: "comments" } %> <%# app/views/comments/create.turbo_stream.erb %> <%= turbo_stream.append "comments", @comment %> <%= turbo_stream.update "comment_form", partial: "comments/form" %> <%# Stimulus: app/javascript/controllers/clipboard_controller.js export default class extends Controller { static targets = ["source"] copy() { navigator.clipboard.writeText(this.sourceTarget.value) } } %>
takeaways: Turbo Drive makes navigation fast; failed forms must return 422
Frames update one region; Streams append, replace or remove elements, even live via broadcasts
Stimulus attaches small JavaScript controllers to HTML with data- attributes
pitfalls: Returning 200 for a failed form submission, so Turbo ignores the re-rendered form with errors.

quiz.q: A link inside turbo_frame_tag "comment_5" is clicked. What does Turbo do with the response?
options: Extracts the frame with id comment_5 and replaces only that frame
Appends the response to the frame
Opens it in a new tab
quiz.explain: Navigation inside a frame is scoped: Turbo swaps in the matching frame from the response.

concepts.name: Authentication with the Rails 8 generator
concepts.summary: Add sign-in with bin/rails generate authentication, has_secure_password, session records and a limit on login attempts.
concepts.why: Rails 8 ships its own authentication, so you can understand and own every line instead of relying on a large gem.
concepts.body:
**Authentication** means checking who a user is, usually by email and password. Rails 8 includes an **authentication generator**, `bin/rails generate authentication`, that writes a complete sign-in system into your app:

- A `User` model with `has_secure_password` and an `email_address` column, plus a `Session` model that stores each login in the database, along with the visitor's network address and browser.
- An `Authentication` concern included in `ApplicationController`, which requires login for every action by default. Opt out per controller with `allow_unauthenticated_access only: %i[index show]`.
- `SessionsController` for sign-in and sign-out, with a **rate limit** of `rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create` so nobody can try thousands of passwords, and `PasswordsController` with a mailer for password resets.
- `Current.user` and `Current.session`: the signed-in user and their session, reachable from anywhere while a request is handled (`Current` is an `ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes` class).

There is deliberately no sign-up flow; you add a registration controller that fits your app.

`has_secure_password` (needs the bcrypt gem) adds `password` and `password_confirmation` attributes that aren't stored. Instead it stores a `password_digest`: a scrambled fingerprint of the password that can be checked but not turned back into it. It also provides `authenticate`. The generator uses `User.authenticate_by(email_address:, password:)`, which takes constant time whether or not the user exists, so attackers can't detect valid emails by timing.

The session's id lives in a long-lasting cookie that is signed (so it can't be forged) and `httponly` (so page scripts can't read it). Signing out deletes the `Session` row, which also makes it easy to log a user out everywhere at once.

For "sign in with Google"-style logins, add OmniAuth; Devise remains an option for apps that need many features out of the box. **Authorization** (what a signed-in user may do) is separate: check ownership in controllers, e.g. `Current.user.articles.find(params[:id])`, or use a gem like Pundit.
concepts.code:
# $ bin/rails generate authentication && bin/rails db:migrate
# app/models/user.rb (generated)
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_secure_password
  has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy
  normalizes :email_address, with: ->(e) { e.strip.downcase }
end
# app/controllers/sessions_controller.rb (generated, abridged)
class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access only: %i[new create]
  rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create,
             with: -> { redirect_to new_session_url, alert: "Try again later." }
  def create
    if user = User.authenticate_by(params.permit(:email_address, :password))
      start_new_session_for user
      redirect_to after_authentication_url
    else
      redirect_to new_session_path, alert: "Try another email address or password."
    end
  end
end
# Your controllers: scope records to the signed-in user (authorization)
class ArticlesController < ApplicationController
  def edit = @article = Current.user.articles.find(params[:id])   # 404 for others' articles
end
takeaways: bin/rails generate authentication creates User, Session, controllers and the Authentication concern
Every action requires login unless allow_unauthenticated_access is used
authenticate_by and rate_limit defend against timing and brute-force attacks
pitfalls: Treating authentication as authorization: a logged-in user can still load other users' records unless you limit queries to their own records.

quiz.q: Why does the generator use User.authenticate_by instead of find_by(...)&.authenticate(...)?
options: It takes the same time whether or not the email exists, preventing user enumeration by timing
quiz.explain: authenticate_by always performs a password hash comparison so response time doesn't reveal valid emails.

concepts.name: Testing Rails apps
concepts.summary: Test models, controllers and full user flows with Minitest, fixtures, integration tests and system tests.
concepts.why: Rails' built-in testing stack lets you change code confidently, and every generator creates test stubs for you.
concepts.body:
Rails uses **Minitest** with Rails-specific helpers. Run everything with `bin/rails test`, a file with `bin/rails test test/models/article_test.rb`, or one test by line: `...article_test.rb:12`. Tests run several at a time and in random order, each inside a database transaction that is rolled back afterwards, so tests don't affect each other.

Kinds of tests:

- **Model tests** (`ActiveSupport::TestCase`): validations, scopes and business methods.
- **Integration tests** (`ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest`): send real requests through routes and controllers, checking several parts together, without a browser: `get articles_url`, `post articles_url, params: {...}`, then `assert_response :success`, `assert_redirected_to`, `assert_select "h1", "Articles"`.
- **System tests** (`ApplicationSystemTestCase`): drive a real web browser, through the Capybara library (`visit`, `fill_in`, `click_on`, `assert_text`). Slowest, so keep them for critical journeys.
- Job and mailer tests: `assert_enqueued_with(job: ...)`, `perform_enqueued_jobs`, `assert_emails 1`.

**Fixtures** are named sample records in `test/fixtures/*.yml`, loaded into the test database before the tests run: `articles(:published)` returns one. They are fast and referenced by name, and associations can point to other fixtures by label. Many teams use factory_bot instead.

Useful helpers: `assert_difference("Article.count", 1) { ... }`, `assert_changes`, `travel_to(Time.zone.local(2025, 1, 1))`, and a `sign_in_as(user)` helper for tests that need a logged-in user.

RSpec (rspec-rails) is a popular alternative with the same concepts and a different way of writing them.
concepts.code:
# test/fixtures/articles.yml
# published:
#   title: Hello
#   slug: hello
#   published: true
#   author: ada          # references users(:ada)

# test/integration/articles_flow_test.rb
require "test_helper"

class ArticlesFlowTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  setup { sign_in_as users(:ada) }     # your test helper that signs in
  test "creates an article" do
    assert_difference("Article.count", 1) do
      post articles_url, params: { article: { title: "New", body: "Text" } }
    end
    assert_redirected_to article_url(Article.last)
    follow_redirect!
    assert_select "h1", "New"
  end
  test "rejects a blank title" do
    post articles_url, params: { article: { title: "" } }
    assert_response :unprocessable_entity
  end
end
takeaways: bin/rails test runs Minitest in parallel with transactional isolation
Integration tests cover routes to views; system tests drive a real browser
Fixtures provide named sample records; assert_difference checks what changed
pitfalls: Writing mostly slow system tests for logic that model or integration tests could cover faster.

quiz.q: Which test type exercises routing, controllers and views through HTTP without a browser?
options: Unit test of the controller class
quiz.explain: ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest sends real requests through the full stack, minus JavaScript and a browser.

concepts.name: Background jobs with Active Job
concepts.summary: Run slow work in the background with Active Job and Solid Queue, with retries, scheduling and recurring tasks.
concepts.why: Sending emails, building exports and calling other services belong in jobs, so requests stay fast and failures can be retried.
concepts.body:
A **background job** is work done outside the request, by a separate process, so the user doesn't wait for it. **Active Job** is Rails' standard way to write one, and **Solid Queue**, the Rails 8 default, stores waiting jobs in the database, so no extra software such as Redis is required. Sidekiq and GoodJob are popular alternatives for running them.

Generate a job with `bin/rails generate job ExportReport`:

```ruby
class ExportReportJob < ApplicationJob
  queue_as :default
  def perform(user, month) ... end
end
```

Enqueue with `ExportReportJob.perform_later(user, "2025-06")`. Arguments are **serialized** (turned into text to store). Active Record objects are stored as **GlobalID** references, like `gid://app/Invoice/42`, and loaded fresh when the job runs, so pass records rather than huge hashes. Schedule with `set(wait: 10.minutes)` or `set(wait_until: ...)`. Mailers have `deliver_later`, which uses Active Job.

Handling failure:

- `retry_on Net::OpenTimeout, wait: :polynomially_longer, attempts: 5` tries again after temporary errors, waiting longer before each attempt (**backoff**).
- `discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError` drops jobs whose records were deleted.
- Make jobs **idempotent**, safe to run twice with the same result, since a job can run again after a crash or retry.

Enqueue jobs after the surrounding transaction commits (use `after_commit` callbacks), or a **worker**, the process that runs jobs, may pick the job up before the data exists.

Run workers with `bin/jobs`; on the live site Solid Queue can run inside the Puma web server (`SOLID_QUEUE_IN_PUMA`) or as its own process. **Recurring tasks** are declared in `config/recurring.yml`. Mission Control Jobs adds a web dashboard for inspecting and retrying jobs. In tests, `perform_enqueued_jobs` runs them inline.
concepts.code:
class SyncInvoiceJob < ApplicationJob
  queue_as :billing
  retry_on Net::OpenTimeout, Faraday::ServerError, wait: :polynomially_longer, attempts: 5
  discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError       # invoice was deleted

  def perform(invoice)                              # re-fetched via GlobalID
    return if invoice.synced_at.present?            # idempotent
    remote_id = BillingApi.push(invoice.as_json)
    invoice.update!(remote_id:, synced_at: Time.current)
  end
end

class Invoice < ApplicationRecord
  after_create_commit -> { SyncInvoiceJob.perform_later(self) }
end

SyncInvoiceJob.set(wait: 10.minutes).perform_later(invoice)

# config/recurring.yml (Solid Queue)
# production:
#   nightly_cleanup:
#     class: CleanupJob
#     schedule: every day at 3am

# $ bin/jobs     # start Solid Queue workers locally
takeaways: perform_later enqueues; records are passed as GlobalIDs and reloaded
retry_on and discard_on declare failure handling; keep jobs idempotent
Solid Queue (default) stores jobs in the database; recurring tasks go in recurring.yml
pitfalls: Enqueuing a job from after_save inside a transaction, so the worker can't find the uncommitted record.

quiz.q: How does Active Job pass an Active Record object argument to a job?
options: As a JSON copy of all attributes
It can't; you must pass the id
As a GlobalID reference, re-fetching the record when the job runs
quiz.explain: GlobalID serialisation stores a reference like gid://app/Invoice/42 and loads the record at execution time.

concepts.name: Caching
concepts.summary: Speed up pages with fragment and Russian-doll caching, low-level Rails.cache, and HTTP conditional GETs.
concepts.why: Caching is the cheapest way to make a slow Rails page fast, if keys and expiry are designed correctly.
concepts.body:
A **cache** saves the result of slow work, such as rendering a page section, so the next request reuses it. Rails relies on **key-based expiration**: each cache key includes the record's id and its `updated_at` time, so when a record changes its key changes and the old entry simply stops being read. You rarely delete cache entries yourself.

**Fragment caching** in views:

```erb
<% cache article do %>
  <%= render article %>
<% end %>
```

**Russian-doll caching** nests fragments: the article fragment contains cached comment fragments. When a comment changes, `belongs_to :article, touch: true` bumps the article's `updated_at`, invalidating the outer fragment while unchanged inner fragments are reused. `render partial: "comment", collection: comments, cached: true` fetches a whole collection's fragments in one read.

**Low-level caching** stores any computed value:

```ruby
Rails.cache.fetch(["stats", user], expires_in: 12.hours) { expensive_query }
```

It returns the cached value or runs the block and stores the result. Cache plain data (numbers, hashes, arrays of ids) rather than Active Record objects or relations.

**HTTP caching** works with the browser: `fresh_when(@article)` or `stale?` add ETag and Last-Modified headers (a version stamp) to the response, and when the browser's next GET request carries the same stamp, the server answers `304 Not Modified` with no body.

The store is configured per environment. Rails 8 uses **Solid Cache** on the live site, a store kept in your database that can hold far more than memory-based caches; Redis and Memcached are alternatives. Caching is off in development until you run `bin/rails dev:cache`.
concepts.code:
<%# app/views/articles/show.html.erb %> <% cache @article do %> <%# key: views/articles/42-20250601... %>

<%= @article.title %>

<%= render partial: "comments/comment", collection: @article.comments, cached: true %> <% end %> <%# app/models/comment.rb: belongs_to :article, touch: true # comment change -> article updated_at bumps %> <%# app/controllers/articles_controller.rb def show @article = Article.find(params[:id]) fresh_when @article # 304 if the client's ETag matches end def stats @stats = Rails.cache.fetch(["article-stats", @article], expires_in: 1.hour) do { views: @article.views.count, readers: @article.views.distinct.count(:user_id) } end end %>
takeaways: Keys include updated_at, so changed records get new keys automatically
Russian-doll caching plus touch: true reuses unchanged inner fragments
Rails.cache.fetch caches computed values; fresh_when enables 304 responses
pitfalls: Caching relations or full Active Record objects instead of plain data, wasting space and returning stale or unloadable objects.

quiz.q: A comment is edited. With touch: true on belongs_to :article, what happens to the cached article fragment?
options: The article's updated_at changes, so its cache key changes and a new fragment is rendered
Nothing; it stays stale until it expires
quiz.explain: touch bumps the parent's timestamp, which is part of the fragment key, so the old entry is no longer used.

concepts.name: Building JSON APIs
concepts.summary: Build JSON APIs with Rails: API-only apps, shaping JSON, error handling, versioning and token authentication.
concepts.why: Rails is a productive back end for mobile apps and JavaScript front ends, and an API needs consistent responses and errors.
concepts.body:
A **web API** is a set of URLs that programs, such as a mobile app, call to read and change data as JSON instead of loading pages. `rails new myapi --api` creates an **API-only** app: controllers inherit from `ActionController::API`, and the parts for cookies, sessions, flash and HTML views are left out. A regular app can serve JSON too, from the same models.

Render JSON with `render json: @article, status: :created`. By default this calls `as_json` on the object. Control the output with:

- `as_json(only: [...], include: { author: { only: :name } })` for simple cases.
- **Jbuilder** templates (`show.json.jbuilder`), which ship with Rails.
- Serializer libraries such as Alba or Blueprinter, or plain Ruby objects with a `to_h`, for larger APIs.

Never send models out whole, or every new column (and private data like password digests) leaks automatically.

Consistent errors: use `rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` to render a JSON 404, and return `422` with `{ errors: record.errors }` for validation failures. Use the right status codes: 201 on create, 204 with `head :no_content` on delete.

Versioning: `namespace :api do namespace :v1 do resources :articles end end` puts controllers in `Api::V1::`.

Authentication: instead of a password, API clients send a **token**, a long random code, in the `Authorization: Bearer ...` header; `authenticate_or_request_with_http_token` reads it. `generates_token_for :api, expires_in: 30.days` on the model creates signed, expiring tokens that `find_by_token_for(:api, token)` verifies; for long-lived random tokens, store only a digest. Limit request rates with `rate_limit` (Rails 7.2+) and return long lists a page at a time, with a gem such as Pagy or with `limit` and `offset`.
concepts.code:
# app/controllers/api/v1/articles_controller.rb
module Api::V1
  class ArticlesController < ActionController::API
    include ActionController::HttpAuthentication::Token::ControllerMethods
    before_action :authenticate!
    rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound, with: -> { render json: { error: "not found" }, status: :not_found }

    def index
      render json: Article.published.includes(:author).limit(50)
                          .as_json(only: %i[id title], include: { author: { only: :name } })
    end

    def create
      article = @user.articles.new(params.expect(article: %i[title body]))
      if article.save then render json: article, status: :created
      else render json: { errors: article.errors }, status: :unprocessable_entity
      end
    end
    private
    def authenticate!
      @user = authenticate_with_http_token { |token, _| User.find_by_token_for(:api, token) }
      head :unauthorized unless @user
    end
  end
end
takeaways: --api apps use ActionController::API with a slimmer middleware stack
Shape JSON explicitly (as_json options, Jbuilder or serializers); don't dump models
Return proper status codes and JSON errors via rescue_from
pitfalls: Rendering models straight to JSON and leaking columns such as password_digest or internal flags.

quiz.q: What does ActionController::API leave out compared to ActionController::Base?
options: View rendering, cookies, sessions and flash support by default
quiz.explain: API controllers drop browser-oriented modules and middleware but keep params, rendering JSON and callbacks.

concepts.name: Concerns and app architecture
concepts.summary: Share behaviour with ActiveSupport::Concern, and decide when to reach for POROs, service objects and form objects.
concepts.why: As apps grow, where to put logic determines whether the codebase stays pleasant or turns into fat models and controllers.
concepts.body:
A **concern** is a module using `ActiveSupport::Concern`, kept in `app/models/concerns` or `app/controllers/concerns`. It packages behaviour that several classes share, such as `Taggable`, `Searchable` or `Archivable`:

```ruby
module Archivable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  included do
    scope :archived, -> { where.not(archived_at: nil) }
  end
  class_methods do
    def archive_all = update_all(archived_at: Time.current)
  end
  def archive! = update!(archived_at: Time.current)
end
```

`included do` runs in the including class (for scopes, associations, validations and callbacks), `class_methods` adds class methods, and plain methods become instance methods. Concerns can depend on other concerns, and Concern resolves the include order for you.

Concerns are good for genuine, cohesive roles. They are bad as a way to hide a 2,000-line model in five files.

Beyond models and controllers, Rails is happy with plain Ruby objects in `app/models` or new directories under `app/` (all autoloaded):

- **POROs** (plain old Ruby objects, classes with no Rails parent) for concepts without a table, e.g. `Invoice::Calculator`.
- **Form objects** with `ActiveModel::Model` and `ActiveModel::Attributes` for forms that span several models or have no table, getting validations and `form_with` support.
- **Service or command objects** for multi-step workflows (`Checkout.new(cart, user).call`), when the work doesn't clearly belong to one model.
- **Query objects** for complex reporting queries.

Prefer rich models first; extract only when a class has several unrelated responsibilities.
concepts.code:
module Archivable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  included do
    scope :archived, -> { where.not(archived_at: nil) }
  end
  class_methods do
    def archive_older_than(age) = where(created_at: ...age.ago).update_all(archived_at: Time.current)
  end
  def archive! = update!(archived_at: Time.current)
end

class Article < ApplicationRecord; include Archivable; end

class Signup                      # form object spanning User + Account
  include ActiveModel::Model
  attr_accessor :email_address, :company
  validates :email_address, :company, presence: true
  def save
    return false unless valid?
    ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
      account = Account.create!(name: company)
      account.users.create!(email_address:, password: SecureRandom.base58(24))
    end
  end
end
takeaways: ActiveSupport::Concern: included do for class-level declarations, class_methods for class methods
Use concerns for cohesive shared roles, not to hide oversized classes
POROs, form objects and service objects live happily in app/ and are autoloaded
pitfalls: Splitting one oversized model into many single-use concerns, which spreads complexity instead of reducing it.

quiz.q: Inside an ActiveSupport::Concern, where should scope :archived go?
quiz.explain: included do runs in the context of the including class, where scope and other macros are available.

concepts.name: Autoloading, Zeitwerk and boot
concepts.summary: Understand how Zeitwerk maps files to constants, how reloading and eager loading work, and how a Rails app starts up.
concepts.why: Autoloading errors and start-up mistakes are confusing until you know the rules Zeitwerk follows.
concepts.body:
Rails apps never `require` their own files. **Zeitwerk** loads them automatically (**autoloading**) by mapping file paths under the autoload folders (`app/*` subfolders, and `lib` via `config.autoload_lib`) to constant names: `app/models/user_profile.rb` must define `UserProfile`, and `app/services/billing/invoice_sync.rb` must define `Billing::InvoiceSync`. Folders become namespaces. Acronyms need an inflection rule (`inflect.acronym "API"`) if you want `API` rather than `Api`.

Modes:
- **Development**: a constant's file is loaded the first time the constant is used. When a file changes, Rails **reloads**: it forgets the autoloaded constants and loads them again on the next request, so your edits show without restarting. Never store a reloadable class somewhere that outlives a reload, such as an initializer or a class-level variable; it would still point at the old version. Use `Rails.application.config.to_prepare` for setup that must run again after each reload.
- **Production** (the live site) and automated test runs: everything is loaded up front at start-up (Rails calls this eager loading, not to be confused with eager loading associations). That is safe when several requests run at once, catches naming mistakes early, and lets the web server's copies of the app share the loaded code.

Run `bin/rails zeitwerk:check` to verify every file defines the expected constant.

**Boot sequence**, what happens when the app starts: `config/boot.rb` sets up Bundler (and Bootsnap's cache of file locations), `config/application.rb` requires the Rails frameworks and defines your `Application` class, `config/environments/*.rb` applies per-environment settings, then the **initializers** in `config/initializers` run in alphabetical order, and **Railties** (gems that hook into Rails) run their own. Finally, everything is loaded up front if that's enabled and the app is ready to serve.

Keep initializers small and free of side effects; heavy work there slows every start-up, test run and deploy.
concepts.code:
# File -> constant mapping that Zeitwerk expects
# app/models/user_profile.rb             -> UserProfile
# app/models/billing/invoice.rb          -> Billing::Invoice
# app/services/payments/stripe_client.rb -> Payments::StripeClient
# lib/pdf_renderer.rb (autoload_lib)     -> PdfRenderer

# config/application.rb
module Blog
  class Application < Rails::Application
    config.load_defaults 8.0
    config.autoload_lib(ignore: %w[assets tasks])
  end
end

# config/initializers/inflections.rb
ActiveSupport::Inflector.inflections(:en) { |i| i.acronym "API" }
# now app/controllers/api/users_controller.rb -> API::UsersController

# config/initializers/payments.rb
Rails.application.config.to_prepare do
  Payments.gateway = Payments::StripeClient.new   # re-run after each code reload
end
# $ bin/rails zeitwerk:check
# Hold on, I am eager loading the application.
# All is good!
takeaways: Zeitwerk maps file paths to constant names; folders are namespaces
Development autoloads and reloads; production loads everything at start-up
Use to_prepare for setup that refers to reloadable classes; check with zeitwerk:check
pitfalls: Storing a reference to an app class in an initializer, which becomes stale after a reload in development.

quiz.q: app/services/pdf/export.rb defines class PdfExport. What happens?
options: Zeitwerk expects Pdf::Export there and raises a naming error when loading
quiz.explain: Zeitwerk derives the expected constant from the path; a mismatch fails, and zeitwerk:check reports it.

concepts.name: Rack and the middleware stack
concepts.summary: See how a request travels from Puma through the Rack middleware stack and the router to a controller, and write your own middleware.
concepts.why: Understanding Rack explains where cookies, sessions, CSRF checks and logging happen, and lets you add behaviour to every request cleanly.
concepts.body:
**Rack** is the standard that connects Ruby web servers and frameworks. A Rack app is any object with a `call(env)` method that returns `[status, headers, body]`, where `env` is a hash describing the request. Rails itself is a Rack app, started from `config.ru`.

A request's journey:
- **Puma**, the web server, accepts the connection and builds the `env`. On the live site, Rails 8 apps put **Thruster** in front of Puma; it adds HTTP/2, compression (sending pages smaller) and fast serving of images and other fixed files.
- The **middleware stack**: a chain of small Rack layers, each wrapping the next. A layer can change the `env`, answer immediately without calling the rest, or change the response on the way back out. `bin/rails middleware` lists them: `ActionDispatch::HostAuthorization`, `Rack::Sendfile`, `ActionDispatch::Static`, `ActionDispatch::Executor`, `Rack::Runtime`, `ActionDispatch::RequestId`, `Rails::Rack::Logger`, `ActionDispatch::ShowExceptions`, `ActionDispatch::Cookies`, `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore`, `ActionDispatch::Flash`, `Rack::MethodOverride`, `Rack::ETag` and more.

- The **router** (`ActionDispatch::Routing::RouteSet`, also a Rack app) matches the path and calls the controller action, which is itself a Rack app at the end of the chain.

Add your own middleware with `config.middleware.use MyMiddleware`, or position it with `insert_before`/`insert_after`, and remove one with `config.middleware.delete`. Middleware suits jobs that apply to every request whatever the controller: timing requests, working out which customer's site is being visited from the hostname, blocking abusive network addresses (often with `rack-attack`), or adding headers.

Routes can also mount any Rack app directly: `mount Sidekiq::Web => "/sidekiq"` or `mount ->(env) { [200, {}, ["ok"]] } => "/ping"`.
concepts.code:
# app/middleware/request_timer.rb
class RequestTimer
  def initialize(app) = @app = app
  def call(env)
    started = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
    status, headers, body = @app.call(env)              # inner layers + Rails
    ms = ((Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - started) * 1000).round(1)
    headers["server-timing"] = "app;dur=#{ms}"
    [status, headers, body]
  end
end
# config/application.rb
#   config.middleware.insert_before Rack::Runtime, RequestTimer
# config/routes.rb: any Rack app can be mounted
#   mount ->(env) { [200, { "content-type" => "text/plain" }, ["pong"]] }, at: "/ping"
# $ bin/rails middleware
# use ActionDispatch::HostAuthorization
# use Rack::Sendfile
# use ActionDispatch::Static
# use ActionDispatch::Executor
# ...
# use RequestTimer
# use Rack::Runtime
# ...
# run Blog::Application.routes
takeaways: A Rack app is call(env) returning [status, headers, body]
Rails is a middleware stack wrapped around the router; bin/rails middleware lists it
Use middleware for behaviour that applies to every request regardless of controller
pitfalls: Putting per-request logic that needs current_user or params into middleware; it runs before routing and controllers.

quiz.q: What must a Rack middleware's call(env) return?
quiz.explain: The Rack spec requires a status, a headers hash and an enumerable body.

concepts.name: Deployment, Puma and performance
concepts.summary: Deploy with Kamal 2, tune Puma's processes and threads, size the database connection pool, and find what's slow in production.
concepts.why: How much traffic a live app handles, and how fast, depends on process and thread settings as much as on code.
concepts.body:
**Deploying** means putting a new version of the app on the servers that visitors use (**production**). Rails 8 apps are deployed as containers with **Kamal 2**: a container packs the app with everything it needs so it runs the same on any server. `config/deploy.yml` lists the servers, where the packed app is stored, and the passwords and keys it needs (`.kamal/secrets`). `kamal setup` prepares fresh servers, and `kamal deploy` builds the package, uploads it, starts the new containers and switches traffic to them through **kamal-proxy** without the site going offline, setting up secure https:// addresses automatically with Let's Encrypt. Accessories run databases or Redis next to the app. Heroku, Render and Fly.io remain alternatives.

**Puma** serves requests with both processes and threads:
- `WEB_CONCURRENCY` sets the number of **workers**, separate processes each running a copy of the app. Use roughly one per CPU core, since Ruby's GVL lets only one thread run Ruby code at a time per process.
- `RAILS_MAX_THREADS` sets the **threads** per worker (default 3 since Rails 7.2). While one thread waits for the database or another service, another can run, so threads raise how many requests a process handles; but they also compete for the GVL, so each request may take longer.
- `preload_app!` loads the app before splitting into workers, so the workers share that memory instead of each loading its own copy.

The database **connection pool** (`pool:` in `database.yml`) is the set of open database connections a process keeps. It must be at least the number of threads that use the database in each process, including Solid Queue threads if they run inside Puma; otherwise threads wait for a connection and time out.

Production checklist: enable **YJIT**, which turns Ruby into fast machine code while it runs (on by default when available); serve images and other fixed files with long cache headers via Thruster (Rails' small front proxy) or a **CDN** (a network of servers near your users that hands out copies of files); keep jobs off the web process for heavy loads; and watch the slowest requests, the **p95 and p99** (the times 95% and 99% of requests beat), not averages. Find the slow parts with an **APM** service or free tools: `rack-mini-profiler`, query logs with `config.active_record.query_log_tags_enabled`, and the Rails log, which shows time spent in views versus Active Record.
concepts.code:
# config/deploy.yml (Kamal 2, abridged)
service: blog
image: acme/blog
servers:
  web: [203.0.113.10, 203.0.113.11]
  job:
    hosts: [203.0.113.12]
    cmd: bin/jobs
proxy:
  ssl: true
  host: blog.example.com
env:
  clear:
    WEB_CONCURRENCY: 4      # ~1 Puma worker per core
    RAILS_MAX_THREADS: 3    # threads per worker
  secret: [RAILS_MASTER_KEY]

# config/database.yml (production excerpt)
#   pool: <%= ENV.fetch("RAILS_MAX_THREADS") { 3 } %>

# $ kamal setup     # first time: install Docker, boot kamal-proxy, deploy
# $ kamal deploy    # zero-downtime rollout
# $ kamal app logs -f
takeaways: Kamal 2 deploys containers with no downtime through kamal-proxy
Puma workers run in parallel; threads overlap waiting time within the GVL
Size the DB pool to at least the threads per process that use the database
pitfalls: Raising RAILS_MAX_THREADS without raising the database pool, causing connection timeouts under load.

quiz.q: A server has 4 cores and CPU-heavy requests. What most increases parallel throughput?
options: More Puma workers (about one per core)
quiz.explain: The GVL limits each process to one running Ruby thread, so parallel CPU work needs more processes.

quiz.q: Puma runs 5 threads per worker and Solid Queue runs 3 threads in the same process. What's the minimum sensible pool size?
quiz.explain: Every thread that may query the database at once needs its own connection: 5 + 3 = 8.
